purpose: Living, shareable knowledge base of truth-filtered peak-performance / flow science tidbits. Designed to iterate weekly; future API for team motivation feeds.
voice: Precise, first-principles, Promethean. No hype. Evidence tiers required.

themes.title: Flow triggers
themes.notes: Challenge–skill balance, clear goals, immediate feedback, deep embodiment, rich environment, high consequences, creativity. Separate Kotler packaging from meta-analytic support.

themes.title: Group flow
themes.notes: Shared goals, equal participation, open communication, blending egos. Popular lists are Speculative until primary evidence is cited.

themes.title: Neurochemistry of ecstasis
themes.notes: Dopamine/norepinephrine/endorphins/anandamide/serotonin cocktail is Stealing Fire framing. Map claims to primary neuro papers and tier honestly.

themes.title: Risk/reward of non-ordinary states
themes.notes: Useful kernel vs romanticizing psychedelics/extreme sports. Always flag Contested safety and dose/context dependence.

themes.title: Training vs chemicals
themes.notes: Prefer skill design, recovery, and trigger engineering over pharmacological shortcuts unless evidence is Established.

tidbits.title: Challenge–skill balance is real, not a slogan
tidbits.claim: Perceived challenge–skill match has a moderate association with flow; clear goals and sense of control are co-antecedents.
tidbits.caveats: Experience-sampling effects weaker than lab/self-report trait measures. Not a universal inverted-U every time. No later meta (through 2026 review) overturns Fong 2015; related work-flow metas still treat job demands/resources and challenge fit as core antecedents.

sources.citation: Fong, C. J., Zaleski, D. J., & Leach, J. K. (2015). The challenge–skill balance and antecedents of flow: A meta-analytic investigation. Journal of Positive Psychology, 10(5).

tidbits.practice: Before one deep block, write a single success criterion and one mid-block feedback signal. Set difficulty one notch above comfortable, not heroic.

tidbits.title: Flow shows selective MPFC downregulation, not blanket frontal shutdown
tidbits.claim: Under experimentally induced flow (challenge matched to skill), medial prefrontal / default-mode regions reliably show relative downregulation, while task-positive areas (e.g., dorsolateral PFC, anterior insula) often show relative upregulation. That selective pattern is Promising support for a hypofrontality *kernel* (less self-monitoring), not for global prefrontal shutdown.
tidbits.caveats: Dietrich 2004 is theoretical. Ulrich imaging samples are men-only arithmetic paradigms; women-only replication still missing. Harmat et al. (fNIRS, Tetris) and broader neural-basis reviews find mixed prefrontal results across methods/tasks — so blanket Transient Hypofrontality Hypothesis remains unsettled. Not a license to shut off frontal lobes with stunts or chemicals.

sources.citation: Dietrich, A. (2004). Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying the experience of flow. Consciousness and Cognition.
Ulrich, M., et al. (2016). Dorsal Raphe Nucleus Down-Regulates Medial Prefrontal Cortex during Experience of Flow. Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience.
Ulrich, M., Niemann, F., & Grön, G. (2022). The neural signatures of the psychological construct “flow”: A replication study. Neuroimage: Reports, 2(4), 100139.
sources.n: 41 men (replication); combined N=64 with prior BOLD sample

tidbits.practice: For a skill you already own, run one uninterrupted bout — phone away, no mid-bout self-critique. Save judgment for after the timer; do not chase ‘frontal shutdown’ with chemicals or stunts.

tidbits.title: Short-term sleep loss taxes attention hard — not a flow hack
tidbits.claim: Short-term total sleep deprivation (<48h) impairs cognition across domains; the largest, most reliable hit is simple attention / vigilance lapses, with smaller or nonsignificant effects on some complex reasoning accuracy measures.
tidbits.caveats: Effect sizes vary by domain (Lim & Dinges 2010: large for attention lapses, small/nonsignificant for reasoning accuracy). Later metas on memory under deprivation/restriction are directionally consistent but do not replace the 2010 map of domain sensitivity. Individual vulnerability varies; caffeine is a partial bandage, not recovery.

sources.citation: Lim, J., & Dinges, D. F. (2010). A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables. Psychological Bulletin, 136(3), 375–389.

tidbits.practice: Before a high-stakes deep-work day, protect a full night of sleep. If already short on sleep, shrink challenge (clearer goals, shorter blocks) instead of stacking stimulants and calling it flow.

tidbits.title: Equal airtime beats the smartest person in the room
tidbits.claim: A group's collective intelligence (c) predicts diverse group-task performance better than the average or maximum individual IQ of its members; c correlates with social sensitivity and more equal conversational turn-taking.
tidbits.caveats: Woolley measures collective problem-solving intelligence, not subjective group-flow state. Sawyer's popular 10-condition group-flow list (blending egos, equal participation, etc.) remains largely qualitative/Speculative as a flow package — equal turn-taking is the kernel with hard Science evidence. Later collective-intelligence work has nuances; do not treat c as a license to ignore expertise on technical tasks.

sources.citation: Woolley, A. W., Chabris, C. F., Pentland, A., Hashmi, N., & Malone, T. W. (2010). Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups. Science, 330(6004), 686–688.

tidbits.practice: In one collaboration today, enforce roughly equal speaking turns: no monologue, no silent spectator. If one person dominates, stop and round-robin the next three moves.

tidbits.title: Deliberate practice is effortful — it is not flow
tidbits.claim: Expert-performance training (deliberate practice) is structured, feedback-rich, and often effortful rather than autotelic; Ericsson contrasts it with flow/peak-experience states. Meta-analysis finds deliberate practice important but incomplete: roughly 14% of performance variance overall, higher in games/music/sports and near-zero in many professions.
tidbits.caveats: Magnitude of the practice–performance link is Contested in the popular sense (10,000-hours theater overclaims). Macnamara et al. 2014 domain splits: ~26% games, ~21% music, ~18% sports, ~4% education, <1% professions. Chemicals/stimulants do not substitute for this structure.

sources.citation: Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T., & Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363–406.

Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608–1618.

tidbits.practice: Split today: one hard deliberate-practice bout (single weakness, immediate feedback, expect effort) and separately one performance/flow bout on a skill you already own. Do not demand flow during the hard reps.

tidbits.title: Unfinished prior work leaves attention residue on the next block
tidbits.claim: When people switch from an unfinished Task A to Task B, attention residue from A impairs performance on B; completing A (or closing it under time pressure) reduces that residue.
tidbits.caveats: Two lab experiments (Leroy 2009), not a multi-lab meta. Mechanism is cognitive, not mystical. Does not prove multitasking is always worse in every field setting, but it is a clean experimental hit against mid-block context switching.

sources.citation: Leroy, S. (2009). Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 109(2), 168–181.

tidbits.practice: Before one deep block, park or finish open loops: write the next physical action for each unfinished task, then leave those tabs closed until the timer ends.

tidbits.title: Classic psychedelics are not a free-pass ecstasis chemical
tidbits.claim: In monitored clinical/research settings, serious adverse events after high-dose classic psychedelics were reported for no healthy participants and roughly 4% of participants with preexisting neuropsychiatric disorders; common acute effects (headache, anxiety, nausea) are frequent but usually self-limited. AE ascertainment is often incomplete, and these rates do not generalize to unsupervised use.
tidbits.caveats: Established for published clinical/research AE rates (Hinkle et al. 2024). Contested as a Stealing Fire DIY flow shortcut: romanticizing set-and-setting theater is not a safety protocol. Johnson, Richards & Griffiths 2008 require screening, preparation, supervision, and follow-up. Recreational risk surfaces (dose uncertainty, psychosis vulnerability, no monitors) sit outside this evidence.

sources.citation: Hinkle, J. T., Graziosi, M., Nayak, S. M., & Yaden, D. B. (2024). Adverse events in studies of classic psychedelics: A systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry, 81(12), 1225–1235.
Johnson, M., Richards, W., & Griffiths, R. (2008). Human hallucinogen research: Guidelines for safety. Journal of Psychopharmacology, 22(6), 603–620.

tidbits.practice: Today, train one non-pharmacological trigger instead of romanticizing chemical ecstasis. If you ever explore a classic psychedelic, treat clinical screening and supervision as non-negotiable — not optional vibe.

tidbits.title: One bout of exercise gives a small, reliable cognitive bump
tidbits.claim: A single session of exercise produces a small but significant overall improvement in cognitive performance (Hedges g ≈ 0.10 across 79 studies). Effects appear during, immediately after, and after a short delay; immediately post-exercise, light-to-moderate intensity tends to help most, and sessions longer than about 20 minutes outperform very short bouts.
tidbits.caveats: Effect is small on average; moderators (intensity, timing, task type, fitness) matter. Not a license to skip sleep or chase maximal intensity before deep work. Catecholamine/BDNF mechanisms are implicated but not proven as the sole pathway. Prefer this over pharmacological arousal shortcuts.

sources.citation: Chang, Y. K., Labban, J. D., Gapin, J. I., & Etnier, J. L. (2012). The effects of acute exercise on cognitive performance: A meta-analysis. Brain Research, 1453, 87–101.

tidbits.practice: Before one deep block, do at least 20 minutes of light-to-moderate aerobic work, then start the cognitive task after a short cool-down (roughly 10–20 minutes), not while still gasping.

tidbits.title: Severe-stress cortisol levels impair flow
tidbits.claim: Exogenous cortisol at a dose matching a severe stressor (20 mg oral) causally reduces flow during a challenging game, supporting an inverted-U: moderate arousal may facilitate flow, but high cortisol impairs it.
tidbits.caveats: Single double-blind crossover experiment (N=64, Pacman blocks). Isolates cortisol from other stress responses; does not map every real-world stressor 1:1. Complements Peifer et al. 2014 JESP endogenous inverted-U under stress. Not a claim that zero stress is optimal.

sources.citation: Peifer, C., Schächinger, H., Engeser, S., & Antoni, C. H. (2015). Cortisol effects on flow-experience. Psychopharmacology, 232, 1165–1173. (Published online 2014)

Peifer, C., Schulz, A., Schächinger, H., Baumann, N., & Antoni, C. H. (2014). The relation of flow-experience and physiological arousal under stress — Can u shape it? Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 53, 62–69.

tidbits.practice: Before deep work, cut one high-cortisol load: skip the doom-scroll, the inbox ambush, or stacking deadlines into the first hour. Aim for moderate arousal, not panic.

tidbits.title: Task-relevant feedback causally raises flow
tidbits.claim: In a controlled HCI experiment, designs with continuous task-relevant feedback produced higher flow ratings than no-feedback or randomized-feedback controls.
tidbits.caveats: Single controlled experiment lineage (Schaffer & Fang 2022 THCI; earlier 2016 SIGHCI timing-game work). Domain is computer tasks/games, not all work. Feedback must map to goals — noise feedback does not help.

sources.citation: Schaffer, O., & Fang, X. (2022). The Feedback Loop of Flow: Controlled Experiment Shows Task-relevant Feedback Increases Flow. AIS Transactions on Human-Computer Interaction, 14(3), 356–389.

tidbits.practice: For one deep block today, invent a continuous scoreboard tied to the actual goal (e.g., tests green, words written, reps completed) — not a mood check or random notification.

tidbits.title: Curiosity recruits dopaminergic learning circuits — not a five-chemical cocktail
tidbits.claim: High-curiosity states enhance memory for the curious material and for incidental items encoded nearby; fMRI links the benefit to anticipatory activity in the SN/VTA–hippocampus dopaminergic circuit.
tidbits.caveats: Gruber et al. 2014 is strong experimental neuroimaging, not a flow induction study. Stealing Fire’s neat dopamine/NE/endorphin/anandamide/serotonin stack remains Speculative packaging — useful kernel is intrinsic curiosity/reward anticipation, not chemical theater.

sources.citation: Gruber, M. J., Gelman, B. D., & Ranganath, C. (2014). States of curiosity modulate hippocampus-dependent learning via the dopaminergic circuit. Neuron, 84(2), 486–496.
Kang, M. J., et al. (2009). The wick in the candle of learning: Epistemic curiosity activates reward circuitry and enhances memory. Psychological Science, 20(8), 963–973.

tidbits.practice: Open one hard block by writing a concrete information gap you actually want answered (one sentence), then work only until that gap closes — curiosity first, stimulant second.

tidbits.title: Micro-breaks restore vigor; they do not reliably unlock hard cognitive performance
tidbits.claim: A meta-analysis of micro-breaks (<10 min) found small improvements in vigor and reduced fatigue, but no significant overall performance gain; any performance signal rose with longer breaks and favored creative/clerical more than demanding cognitive tasks.
tidbits.caveats: Established for well-being (vigor/fatigue). Contested as a productivity hack for deep cognition — do not treat 90-second phone scrolls as recovery or as proof of a rigid 90-minute ultradian cognitive law.

sources.citation: Albulescu, P., Macsinga, I., Rusu, A., Sulea, C., Bodnaru, A., & Tulbure, B. T. (2022). Give me a break! A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLOS ONE, 17(8), e0272460.

tidbits.practice: After one focused bout, take a real micro-break that drops the task (stand, breathe, walk) for a few minutes — not inbox or social feed — then return.

lane.prometheus: Peak states, flow, focus, ecstasis, training design
lane.helix: Longevity / lasting-longer biology — hand off, do not duplicate
